LESSON 1 • Chronology, Geography & Contrast With Britain c. AD 900

Building the Round City of Baghdad (AD 750–900)

Key Enquiry: Why was the Round City of Baghdad built, and how big did it grow?
[1.1] AD 610–762: Rapid Spread of Early Islam & Choosing the River Tigris
“Why did Caliph al-Mansur build his capital on the River Tigris?”

Beginning in Arabia, the faith of Islam spread swiftly across wide lands. In AD 750, the Abbasid [uh-BASS-id] family took charge of this empire, led by a Caliph. In AD 762, Caliph al-Mansur [al-man-SOOR] searched for a safe central spot for his capital. He chose a fertile green bend on the River Tigris.

Deep canals linked the Tigris straight to the River Euphrates. Fresh water fed lush date palms and golden wheat fields. Round woven-reed quffa [KOOF-uh] boats brought silk and spices, while Silk Road camel caravans met there.

[1.2] AD 762–766: 100,000 Builders & the Round City of Peace
“How was the circular Round City of Baghdad designed and built?”

Al-Mansur gathered 100,000 bricklayers and diggers to raise the circular Round City of Baghdad. Architects first traced a circle two kilometres wide in flaming cotton seeds! Builders then baked millions of mud bricks for thick double walls and a deep moat. Al-Mansur named his capital Madinat al-Salam [mah-DEE-nat al-sah-LAHM], meaning City of Peace.

Four guarded iron gates pierced the walls, named Kufa, Basra, Khorasan, and Syria. Straight market streets led towards the open centre. Right at the heart stood the Great Mosque beside the Green Dome Palace.

[1.3] c. AD 900: One Million Citizens vs Anglo-Saxon Britain
“How did Baghdad around AD 900 compare with towns in Anglo-Saxon Britain?”

Busy markets, bathhouses, and gardens soon spread beyond the Round City walls. By AD 900, bustling Baghdad was home to nearly one million people! Families strolled down paved streets beside cool canals and studied inside grand libraries.

Meanwhile, towns in Anglo-Saxon Britain around AD 900 looked tiny by comparison. Even major English towns like London or Winchester held only 5,000 to 10,000 people. Most British families lived in smoky timber huts with thatched roofs. Muddy village lanes showed how huge Baghdad truly was!

LESSON 2 • Historical Significance & Cultural Exchange

Paper & The House of Wisdom (c. AD 800–1000)

Key Enquiry: How did cheap paper and Baghdad’s House of Wisdom save world knowledge?
[2.1] c. AD 786–833: Harun al-Rashid, Al-Ma’mun & the Paper Revolution
“How did Samarkand paper-making transform Baghdad’s book markets?”

Under Caliph Harun al-Rashid and his son Caliph al-Ma'mun [al-mah-MOON], Baghdad drew thinkers from afar. Together they expanded a royal library into the House of Wisdom, or Bayt al-Hikma [bayt al-HIK-mah]. Via the Silk Road city of Samarkand, craftworkers learned Chinese paper-making. Watermills beat old cotton and linen rags into smooth, cheap paper.

Across Europe, scribes still scraped costly calfskin parchment from whole cattle herds! Cheap rag paper transformed Baghdad's book markets. Soon over 100 bookshops buzzed in the Paper Sellers' Market with poetry and star charts.

[2.2] c. AD 830–900: The Translation Movement & Hunayn ibn Ishaq
“How did the Translation Movement rescue and improve ancient world knowledge?”

Al-Ma'mun sent messengers to buy rare ancient scrolls from Greece, Persia, and India. Inside the House of Wisdom, the Translation Movement rescued fragile books before they crumbled. Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars worked together turning Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit texts into Arabic.

Their star translator was Hunayn ibn Ishaq [hoo-NAYN ib-in is-HAHK], a gifted Christian doctor. Stories say al-Ma'mun paid him the weight of every finished book in gold! Baghdad's scholars never copied old writers blindly. Instead, they tested every claim and fixed mistakes.

[2.3] c. AD 800–900: Visionary Women Patrons — Fatima al-Fihri & Queen Zubayda
“How did Fatima al-Fihri and Queen Zubayda shape the Islamic Golden Age?”

Generous women also shaped the Islamic Golden Age as visionary patrons funding public works. In AD 859, Fatima al-Fihri spent her family wealth in Fez, Morocco. She founded al-Qarawiyyin [al-kah-rah-wee-YEEN], a grand mosque and teaching college. Students still gather there today to study maths, star maps, and law!

Earlier in Baghdad, Queen Zubayda [zoo-BAY-dah], wife of Harun al-Rashid, planned a desert water lifeline. Thirsty pilgrims walking the hot Hajj road to Mecca needed water. Zubayda paid masons to dig stone wells and pools that saved thousands!

LESSON 3 • Significance & History of Science

Zero, Astrolabes & Free Hospitals (c. AD 820–1050)

Key Enquiry: What amazing discoveries did Baghdad’s doctors and scientists make?
[3.1] c. AD 820–1206: Zero, Algebra, Astrolabes & the Elephant Clock
“How did Baghdad’s maths, astrolabes, and clocks advance world science?”

In Baghdad's House of Wisdom, Muhammad al-Khwarizmi [al-kwah-RIZ-mee] championed Hindu-Arabic numerals from 0 to 9. Using zero, called sifr [SIF-er], made big sums far easier than clumsy Roman numerals! His maths book al-Jabr gave us algebra, and his own name gave us algorithm.

Makers like Mariam al-Asturlabi [al-as-toor-LAH-bee] crafted brass astrolabes to map bright stars. Travellers held them up to check prayer times, sail seas, and find Mecca. Engineer al-Jazari [al-jah-ZAH-ree] also built clocks like his Elephant Water Clock. Hidden floats clashed brass cymbals every half hour to advance science!

[3.2] c. AD 965–1040: Ibn al-Haytham’s Light Proof & Free Bimaristans
“What did Ibn al-Haytham prove about light, and how did bimaristans help?”

Ancient Greek writers once claimed invisible rays shot out of human eyes to see! Scientist Ibn al-Haytham [IB-in al-HAY-thum] doubted that story and tested light carefully. Inside a dark room with a tiny hole, he built a pinhole camera obscura. He proved light travels in straight lines into our eyes, inspiring modern cameras!

Islamic cities also built free teaching hospitals called bimaristans [bee-MAH-rih-stahnz] for rich and poor alike. Each bimaristan had clean wards, cool fountains, and a stocked pharmacy. Recovering patients even got clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home!

[3.3] c. AD 900–1013: Master Doctors Al-Razi & Al-Zahrawi
“How did al-Razi and al-Zahrawi help sick people heal well?”

Before building Baghdad's hospital, chief doctor al-Razi [al-RAH-zee] hung fresh meat across town. He picked the spot where meat rotted slowest because the air was cleanest! Careful bedside notes helped al-Razi tell measles apart from smallpox. Trained nurses served healthy meals to help sick people recover.

In Spain around AD 1000, royal surgeon al-Zahrawi [al-zah-RAH-wee] wrote an illustrated medical guide. He drew over 200 surgical tools, including forceps, scalpels, and delicate bone saws. He also discovered catgut stitches that dissolved safely inside wounds as patients began to heal!

LESSON 4 • Consequence, Trade & Global Connections

Silk Road Caravans, Dhows & Viking Coins (c. AD 850–1000)

Key Enquiry: How did Baghdad’s traders connect the world all the way to Britain?
[4.1] c. AD 850–1000: Covered Bazaars, Silk Caravans & Roadside Caravanserais
“How did camel trails and walled inns supply Baghdad’s busy markets?”

Baghdad sat where Asia, Africa, and Europe met, making its markets world famous. Shaded bazaars, or souks, smelled of Indian pepper, cardamom, and sweet cinnamon. Stalls gleamed with Chinese silk, white porcelain, Persian rugs, and blown glass. Long caravans of two-humped camels crossed hot Silk Road desert trails.

Every thirty kilometres along the road stood a walled inn called a caravanserai [kar-uh-VAN-suh-ry]. Locked brick gates kept traders safe from desert bandits at night. Tired camels drank cool well water while merchants shared spiced stews by firelight!

[4.2] c. AD 850–1000: Indian Ocean Dhow Ships & Paper Sakk Cheques
“How did wooden dhows and paper sakk cheques boost long-distance trade?”

River boats also carried crates south down the Tigris to the busy sea port of Basra. Sailors loaded wooden dhow [DOW] ships built from planks stitched tightly with coconut rope! Tall triangular sails caught ocean winds across the Indian Ocean towards India and China. Captains steered safely at night by checking star heights with brass astrolabes.

Carrying heavy coin sacks on long-distance trade risked bandit or pirate attacks. Clever Baghdad bankers solved this by writing signed paper slips called a sakk [SAHK]. Merchants cashed them safely afar, giving English our word cheque!

[4.3] c. AD 774–1000: Viking Silver Dirhams in Jorvik & King Offa’s Gold Coin
“What proves Baghdad’s trade coins reached Viking Jorvik and Anglo-Saxon Britain?”

Silver trade coins struck for Baghdad's caliphs even reached snowy Scandinavia and Britain! Pure Abbasid silver dirhams [DEER-hamz] with Arabic script flowed north up Russian rivers. Vikings prized this trusted silver for buying furs and swords. They even buried shining dirham hoards near Jorvik [YOR-vik], modern York!

Even earlier, in Anglo-Saxon Britain, King Offa of Mercia admired Islamic gold coins. Around AD 774, Offa minted a famous gold coin copying an Abbasid Arabic dinar. Swirling Arabic letters beside Offa's name prove how far Baghdad's trade reached!

LESSON 5 • Similarity, Difference & Cultural Life

Courtyards, Tilework & Chess in Baghdad (c. AD 900)

Key Enquiry: What was everyday family life like in Baghdad around AD 900?
[5.1] c. AD 900: Cool Courtyard Houses, Windcatchers & Public Hammams
“How did Baghdad’s homes and hammams keep families cool and clean?”

Summer afternoons in Iraq blazed hot, yet Baghdad's builders kept homes wonderfully cool. Thick brick walls sheltered shaded inner courtyards splashed by stone fountains and orange trees. Above the roofs rose tall windcatcher towers, called badgirs [bad-GEERZ], facing the breeze. They scooped cool outdoor air down indoors while pushing hot air out!

Keeping clean mattered deeply before daily prayers and families' meals. Every district had steamed public bathhouses called hammams [hah-MAHMZ] with tiled hot and cool rooms. Bathers scrubbed with olive-oil soap bars and splashed sweet rosewater!

[5.2] c. AD 900: Citrus Orchards, Spiced Kitchens & Geometric Mosque Art
“What new foods and art styles flourished in Baghdad around AD 900?”

Around AD 900, canal waterwheels fed lush orchards around Baghdad filled with tasty new foods. Farmers grew tangy lemons, sweet oranges, purple aubergines, green spinach, and ruby pomegranates. Cooks simmered spiced stews with crushed almonds and cane sugar. Families served warm dishes on shiny metallic lustreware bowls.

Inside mosques, art styles avoided human or animal statues so worshippers honoured God alone. Using compasses, tilers made eight-pointed geometric stars and curling arabesque [ar-uh-BESK] leaf vines. Sacred Arabic calligraphy from the Qur'an completed every wall in calm symmetry!

[5.3] c. AD 900: Silk Tiraz Robes, Glass Mosque Lamps & Shatranj Chess
“How did people in Baghdad dress, light their homes, and play?”

Skilled workshops helped people in Baghdad dress finely and light their homes. Royal looms wove bright silk robes trimmed with embroidered Arabic name bands called tiraz [tee-RAHZ]. Master glassblowers also gilded enamelled glass mosque lamps inscribed with glowing verses.

When evening breezes cooled the courtyard, families sat on woven carpets. Guests sipped sweet fruit syrups with rosewater and loved to play strategy games! Everyone prized shatranj [shat-RANJ], the ancient board game that became chess. Clever winners cried Shah mat, giving English our word checkmate!

LESSON 6 • Causation, Consequence & Lasting Legacy

The 1258 Siege of Baghdad & Surviving Ideas

Key Enquiry: Why did Baghdad fall in 1258, and how did its ideas survive?
[6.1] January–February AD 1258: Hulagu Khan & the Mongol Siege of Baghdad
“Why did Baghdad fall to Hulagu Khan’s Mongol army in February 1258?”

Over centuries, the huge Abbasid Empire split into smaller rival kingdoms. Baghdad stayed proud in learning, yet its weak army could not guard wide borders. In January 1258, a vast Mongol army led by Hulagu Khan [hoo-LAH-goo KAHN] marched from Central Asia. Thousands of horsemen surrounded Baghdad along both banks of the River Tigris.

Mongol engineers built giant wooden trebuchets [TREB-yoo-shets] that hurled heavy boulders at Baghdad's brick walls. In February 1258, Mongol troops stormed through the broken walls. Fires ruined palaces, canals, and the House of Wisdom, ending Abbasid rule.

[6.2] Cairo, Córdoba & Toledo: Why Golden Age Knowledge Survived
“How did cities like Cairo, Córdoba, and Toledo rescue Golden Age knowledge?”

Did Golden Age knowledge vanish in 1258 when Baghdad's library burned? Thankfully not, because paper copies sat safely in cities like Cairo, Damascus, and Samarkand! Far west in Islamic Spain, called Al-Andalus [al-AN-duh-loos], Córdoba [KOR-doh-bah] shone with street lamps and seventy libraries. Rulers there also built Granada's carved Alhambra palace.

Next, Spanish Toledo became Europe's bridge for rescuing Arabic science. Muslim, Jewish, and Christian translators worked side by side there. Turning al-Khwarizmi, Ibn al-Haytham, and Ibn Sina [IB-in SEE-nah] into Latin helped spark Europe's Renaissance!

[6.3] From 1258 to Today: Arabic Words & Ideas in Our Everyday Lives
“How does the Early Islamic Golden Age still shape our lives today?”

Today, the Early Islamic Golden Age still shapes our lives at school and home! Writing digits 0 to 9, solving algebra, or running a phone algorithm uses Baghdad's maths. Ibn al-Haytham's light tests led straight to glasses, microscopes, and smartphone cameras. Clean hospital wards and pharmacies also build on Islamic medicine.

You even speak everyday Arabic words like zero, chemistry, sugar, lemon, and orange! Cosy home words like sofa and cotton arrived through Arabic trade too. Though Baghdad's walls fell in 1258, Golden Age ideas live on!

KEY STAGE 2 ILLUSTRATED GLOSSARY SYLLABLE HELPERS & DEFINITIONS

Historian's Word Bank (24 Essential Terms)

Clap the italic syllables out loud together to master new historical words with confidence!

Caliph Ca-liph
The supreme political and spiritual leader who ruled the early Islamic Empire (the Caliphate).
Abbasid Ab-ba-sid
The ruling family who took charge of the Islamic Empire in AD 750 and built Baghdad as their capital.
Canals Ca-nals
Human-made waterways dug between rivers to irrigate green farmlands and carry trading boats.
Madinat al-Salam Ma-di-nat al-Sa-lam
Arabic for "City of Peace", the official name Caliph al-Mansur gave to the Round City of Baghdad in AD 762.
House of Wisdom House of Wis-dom
Baghdad’s famous royal library and research academy (Bayt al-Hikma), expanded by Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun.
Parchment Parch-ment
Expensive writing sheets scraped from calfskin or sheepskin, used in medieval Europe long after Baghdad used paper.
Samarkand Sa-mar-kand
A wealthy Silk Road oasis city in Central Asia through which Chinese rag paper-making spread to Baghdad.
Translation Movement Trans-la-tion Move-ment
The organised effort in Baghdad to translate Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit science and medical scrolls into Arabic.
Algebra Al-ge-bra
A branch of mathematics using balanced equations and unknown numbers, named after al-Khwarizmi’s book al-Jabr.
Algorithm Al-go-rith-m
A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a maths or computer problem, named after Muhammad al-Khwarizmi.
Astrolabe As-tro-labe
A finely engraved brass star instrument used to tell the time, navigate oceans, and find the direction of Mecca.
Camera Obscura Ca-me-ra Ob-scu-ra
A pitch-dark pinhole room used by Ibn al-Haytham to prove that light travels in straight lines into our eyes.
Bazaar Ba-zaar
A bustling covered market street (also called a souk) lined with stalls selling silk, spices, carpets, and glass.
Caravanserai Car-a-van-se-rai
A walled roadside inn with courtyard wells built every thirty kilometres so Silk Road camel caravans could rest safely.
Dhow Dhow
A wooden Arab sailing ship built from stitched planks and rigged with triangular sails for crossing the Indian Ocean.
Sakk Sakk
A signed paper payment note from Abbasid bankers that merchants cashed in distant cities — origin of our word cheque.
Windcatcher Wind-catch-er
A tall rooftop cooling tower (badgir) that funnels fresh breezes down into shaded courtyard rooms during hot summers.
Hammam Ham-mam
A steamed neighbourhood bathhouse with hot and cool tiled rooms where people washed with soap and rosewater.
Geometric Ge-o-met-ric
Art built from mathematical shapes like interlocking stars, circles, and polygons drawn carefully with rulers and compasses.
Arabesque Ar-a-besque
Flowing Islamic patterns of curling stems, leaves, and flowers that weave smoothly across tiles, stone, and metalwork.
Siege Siege
Surrounding a walled city with an army and catapults to cut off supplies and break through its defences.
Trebuchet Treb-u-chet
A powerful medieval wooden catapult that used a heavy dropping counterweight to hurl giant boulders at stone or brick walls.
Al-Andalus Al-An-da-lus
Medieval Islamic Spain and Portugal, famed for great libraries and palaces in Córdoba, Toledo, and Granada’s Alhambra.
Renaissance Re-nais-sance
Europe’s lively rebirth of science, medicine, and art from the 1300s, fuelled partly by Arabic books translated into Latin.

MASTER CHRONOLOGICAL SPINE c. AD 750 TO AD 1258

10 Turning Points Across Early Islamic Baghdad

AD 750 & 762
Abbasids & The Round City: Caliph al-Mansur founds geometric Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace") on the River Tigris.
c. AD 774–905
Offa’s Coin & Viking Dirhams: Islamic gold and silver trade coins reach Mercia and Viking hoards in Yorkshire and Lancashire.
c. AD 794
Baghdad’s First Paper Mills: Cotton and linen rag paper replaces costly parchment, fuelling 100+ bookshops.
c. AD 813–833
House of Wisdom Peak: Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars translate Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit scrolls into Arabic.
c. AD 820
Al-Khwarizmi & Algebra: Pioneers al-Jabr (algebra) and 0–9 place-value numerals; his name gives us "algorithm".
c. AD 850–900
Silk Roads, Dhows & Cheques: Caravanserais, monsoon dhows, and paper sakk ("cheques") link China, India, Africa, and Iraq.
c. AD 900
Al-Razi & Free Bimaristans: Free teaching hospitals open clean wards; Al-Razi distinguishes smallpox from measles.
c. AD 950–964
Astrolabes & Al-Sufi’s Stars: Mariam al-Asturlabi crafts brass astrolabes and Al-Sufi records the Andromeda Galaxy.
c. AD 1011–1025
Optics & Canon of Medicine: Ibn al-Haytham proves how vision works with pinhole cameras; Ibn Sina writes Canon of Medicine.
AD 1258 & Beyond
Mongol Siege & Global Legacy: Hulagu Khan captures Baghdad, yet copies in Cairo, Maragheh, and Spain spark Europe’s Renaissance.
Big Picture Historian Discussion

1. Direct British Contrast (c. AD 900): Compare streets, libraries, hospitals, and food in Baghdad with King Alfred’s Wessex or Viking Jorvik!
2. Shared Human Heritage: How did Baghdad rescue Greek and Indian learning and pass new discoveries on to modern science?
